title: Ethernet PHY (Physical Layer) interface
summary: The Ethernet PHY (Physical Layer) handles the physical transmission of Ethernet frames. MII (Media Independent Interface) connects MAC to PHY: 4-bit data path, 2.5/25/125 MHz clock. RMII (Reduced MII): 2-bit data path, 50 MHz clock. GMII (Gigabit MII): 8-bit data path, 125 MHz clock. RGMII (Reduced GMII): 4-bit data path, 125 MHz clock (double data rate). SGMII (Serial GMII): serial, 1.25 Gbps. Auto-negotiation: PHYs advertise capabilities (speed, duplex) via FLP (Fast Link Pulse) bursts.

structure.meaning: 4-bit data (TXD/RXD), TX_EN, RX_DV, TX_CLK, RX_CLK, CRS, COL, MDIO, MDC. 2.5 MHz (10Mbps), 25 MHz (100Mbps).
2-bit data (TXD/RXD), TX_EN, CRS_DV, REF_CLK (50 MHz). Reduces pin count.
4-bit data, 125 MHz clock (DDR: both edges). Reduces pin count for gigabit.
Serial: 1.25 Gbps differential pair. For 1000BASE-X (fiber) or 1000BASE-T.
FLP (Fast Link Pulse) bursts advertise capabilities. Next pages for extended capabilities (10GBASE-T, etc.).
Management Data I/O: serial interface for reading/writing PHY registers (clause 22 or clause 45).

notes: MII is the standard interface between MAC and PHY.
RGMII is the most common interface for gigabit Ethernet.
Auto-negotiation is essential for interoperability (speed/duplex matching).
PHYs handle encoding (8b/10b, 64b/66b), scrambling, and physical signaling.
Modern PHYs support Energy Efficient Ethernet (EEE) for power saving.
